gao-gaoreports-gao-05-306r:
Activities of the Amtrak Inspector General, GAO-05-306R of March 4, 2005, is a letter that weighs a merger of two watch shops. GAO once urged that small watch shops join big ones to gain staff, skill, and free rein. The Amtrak watch shop and the Transportation watch shop share the same rail beat. A join would pool their cash and crews.

Congress asked GAO to look close at what the Amtrak shop does. The letter maps its audits and probes. It weighs the gains a join could bring, and the weak points a join must guard. Scale and depth are the prize; loss of a rail-only eye is the risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-316r:
Air Force Assessment of the Joint Strike Fighter's Aerial Refueling Method, GAO-05-316R of March 14, 2005, is a letter on a small choice with fleet-wide reach. The jet plan, priced at $245 billion, builds three kin jets for three services. Shared parts are meant to cut cost. Yet the Air Force jet would drink fuel in flight by a boom, while its Navy and Marine kin use a probe and basket.

A Senate panel asked why the split stands. GAO lays out the Air Force's grounds. It prices a switch to one shared way. It weighs the gains and losses in war use if the switch were made.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-396r:
Financial Audit, GAO-05-396R of June 9, 2005, is a side note on one link in the chain that builds the nation's own books. The Treasury and the budget office must give the President and Congress audited sums for the whole U.S. government each year. GAO audits those sums. Each agency backs its share with a signed letter that vows its facts are true.

GAO read the Transportation arm's letter for fiscal year 2004 in five fields. They are the marks, the size caps, the vows, the sum of slips left unfixed, and the trust each vow can bear. The aim is firm letters in years to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-506r:
GAO-05-506R, a letter GAO issued on June 10, 2005, transmits its read of audit reports for the Gold Star Wives of America. The corporation honors the memory of those who served the United States. It also works to better the lives of their children. Two fiscal years are covered, ended May 31, 2004, and May 31, 2003.

Chartered corporations must show their assets and liabilities in yearly statements, with fair detail on income and costs. An independent accountant must audit the statements each year. GAO read the statements and both audit reports. It checked figures with analytical procedures and held brief talks with the auditor about better reporting. No breach of the law's reporting rules was found. The auditors said the statements were fairly presented under standard accounting principles. GAO performed no audit of its own.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-596r:
The Commerce Department's fiscal year 2004 representation letter draws the lightest touch in this set: GAO-05-596R, dated July 14, 2005. The letter backs the audit of the government's financial statements for that year. GAO reviewed five key areas, as it did for every large agency. Only one of the five needed improvement here.

The letter included 27 of the 29 standard representations from the audit manual that applied to the department. Of the other 2, one was partial and one was absent. GAO called the matter easy to address. It made a single recommendation to the chief financial officer: ensure that future letters include every applicable representation in full. A second recommendation went to the inspector general, to work with the department and its outside auditors. In their comments, the deputy finance chief and the inspector general agreed with the findings. Both offices said they will act on them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-606r:
One of the fiscal year 2004 management representation letter reports covers the Small Business Administration: GAO-05-606R, June 23, 2005. SBA's letter helps underpin the government's consolidated financial statements. GAO checked it against five key areas and found fault in one. The letter lacked a complete summary of unadjusted misstatements. It also failed to split errors on government accounts from errors on public accounts.

GAO asked SBA's Chief Financial Officer to include a full summary whenever uncorrected errors exist. It also asked the Acting Inspector General, with the outside audit firm, to help the agency meet the standard. Both offices said they would work to fix the gap.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-636r:
Early word on the science campaigns behind the nuclear stockpile arrives in GAO letter GAO-05-636R, sent April 29, 2005. Since testing stopped in 1992, six campaigns supply the data and computer models used to certify aging warheads. The two lead campaigns study the first and second stages of a blast. Together the six cost about $5.8 billion from fiscal 2001 to 2004.

The lead pair have missed the goals set in 1999, though many smaller milestones were met. Certification targets slipped from 2005-2010 to 2010-2014, hurt by delays at two big test facilities. Planning became uniform only in 2003, and plans still link goals to tasks weakly. A final report was due in December 2005.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-646r:
Arrest histories of jailed illegal immigrants are tallied in GAO letter GAO-05-646R, dated May 9, 2005. GAO studied 55,322 people held in prisons or jails in fiscal 2003 whom immigration records showed entered the country illegally. Their rap sheets list at least 459,614 arrests, about 8 per person, and roughly 700,000 offenses, about 13 each. Nearly all had more than one arrest.

Drug and immigration offenses made up about 45 percent of the total. Property crimes were about 15 percent and violent crimes about 12 percent. Eighty percent of arrests fell in California, Texas, and Arizona. GAO stresses the counts are floors, since some states report only first arrests to the FBI file used.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-746r:
In a letter report, GAO-05-746R (June 30, 2005), GAO updated the money record for hazardous waste programs. The main program is Superfund, run by the Environmental Protection Agency. Two health bodies and a brownfields program also draw on the same funds. Congress asked for totals for fiscal years 1993 to 2005.

The letter gives both funds voted and funds spent for each program. Past GAO work had covered the years up to 2002. This update extends the series and splits out sums once buried in the Superfund total. It also notes that the taxes that once fed the trust fund ended in 1995. Later money came from cost recoveries, interest, fines, and general funds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-756r:
A small defense office and its unclear needs are covered by GAO-05-756R, a letter dated August 25, 2005. The office accounts for troops missing from past wars. It was set up in July 1993. Its work first centered on the Vietnam War. Congress later widened its tasks and voiced worry that it lacked staff and funds.

GAO found the mission has grown to cover past and current conflicts. The office also now leads policy on rescuing live troops. Staff and fund levels have risen only slightly over the years. Congress set floor levels in 2002 tied to the budget for fiscal year 2003. But records gave no clear floor for military staff. GAO said a fresh assessment should pin down what the office needs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-816r:
An insurance antitrust shield is briefed in GAO-05-816R, a letter dated July 28, 2005. The McCarran-Ferguson Act exempts much insurance work from federal antitrust law. GAO briefed congressional staff on May 26, 2005. The letter sends the briefing slides. GAO assessed which insurance practices might break antitrust law without the shield. It also mapped state antitrust powers over insurance.

The briefing rests on a March 2005 GAO legal opinion. That opinion sorted which acts courts have found exempt. The letter's own title gives the bottom line: the final effects of the exemption on insurer activity are unclear. Readers get the practice review and the state-law survey in slide form. The record frames the debate for lawmakers weighing the shield.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-256r:
A small retail test in military grocery stores is sized up in GAO-06-256R, a letter report dated December 22, 2005. Commissaries sell food and home goods at cost plus a 5 percent surcharge. Exchanges run the base retail stores and send most profits to recreation programs. In fiscal years 2000 through 2004 that dividend topped $300 million a year. A 2005 law let commissaries sell film, throwaway cameras, and phone cards in at least 10 stores. Exchange backers feared the shift would cut their dividend. The law told GAO to test that fear.

The title gives GAO's forecast: the harm would likely be negligible. The pilot items are a thin slice of exchange sales. A small dip in those sales cannot move a dividend of that size by much. The letter settles a turf dispute with arithmetic. It shows how a feared loss shrinks when set against the full flow of profits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-366r:
A reusable tag that costs about $100 each should not be thrown away. Letter report GAO-06-366R of March 8, 2006, studies active radio frequency identification tags in defense shipping. The Defense Department uses such tags to track cargo and stock. Poor tracking can hide loss or theft. It can also waste millions on needless purchases.

GAO observed that active tags were not being sent back for reuse as a routine. This report checks the reuse policy and how well tags were tracked. Better use of the tags, GAO said, could avoid millions in needless buys. Readers see a small device tied to a large logistics problem.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-466r:
Aid compacts take time to sign, and unspent aid money raises budget questions. Letter GAO-06-466R, dated February 21, 2006, analyzes future obligations of the Millennium Challenge Corporation. The corporation aids countries that show a commitment to just rule, economic freedom, and investing in people. It received over $4.2 billion in funds for fiscal years 2004 through 2006, most of it set aside for compact aid to those countries.

By January 2006, eight compacts had been signed or approved, and they obligated about $1.5 billion of the funds the corporation had received. That left a balance of about $2.3 billion still unobligated. GAO models how fast that balance could be spent under two scenarios, one with higher cost compacts and one with lower cost compacts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-506r:
Theatre on a national stage is the mission of this chartered corporation. Letter GAO-06-506R, dated March 14, 2006, reviews the audit of the American National Theatre and Academy. The reports cover fiscal years ended June 30, 2003 and 2002. The corporation presents theatrical productions. It works to stir public interest in drama and to develop the art and technique of the theatre.

Chartered corporations must file yearly financial statements under federal law. An independent public accountant must audit them. GAO read the statements, notes, and auditor's report. It found no reportable instance of noncompliance. The auditors said the statements were presented fairly under U.S. accounting principles.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-576r:
Six months after Katrina, New Orleans faced hard choices about rebuilding its hospitals. Letter report GAO-06-576R, dated March 28, 2006, reports the state of the city's health care system. The storm made landfall on August 29, 2005. Flooding followed levee failures. The Medical Center of Louisiana at New Orleans closed after extensive damage. It was the area's main safety net hospital and only Level I trauma center. About half its patients were uninsured.

GAO gathered estimates of available health care services. It reviewed state and local plans to rebuild the system. It also collected damage assessments and repair cost estimates for the medical center. Federal funding eligibility is covered.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-686r:
Radiation experts' finances are reviewed in GAO-06-686R, a GAO letter dated May 12, 2006. The National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements is a federally chartered corporation. It issues information and advice on radiation protection in the public interest. Federal law obliges chartered groups to present their assets, debts, income, and costs in annual statements. An independent public accountant must audit those statements each year.

GAO examined the audit reports for the council's fiscal year 2003. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance with the reporting rules in the law. The auditor had judged the statements fairly presented under United States accounting principles. GAO's letter conveys that finding to Congress as part of its charter oversight. The council's science work is outside the letter's scope.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-736r:
Housing for Air Force families in Germany is questioned in GAO-06-736R, a letter report dated May 19, 2006. The Air Force planned to build 233 housing units on Spangdahlem Air Base at a cost of $131.3 million over fiscal years 2006 through 2008. It also planned 270 build-to-lease units nearby, at $32,888 per unit each year over 20 years. A 2006 law required the Air Force to report its plan to Congress first.

GAO found limits in the data behind the plan. An updated analysis could change the overall housing picture for the base. Some limits the Air Force cited on leased units may have been overstated, and some may no longer exist. GAO also found that the Air Force did not always follow its own life-cycle guidance. The letter urges a fresh look.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-776r:
Risks in buying military space systems fill GAO-06-776R, a letter report GAO issued on June 1, 2006. The Defense Department expected to spend nearly $7 billion in fiscal year 2007 on space-based capabilities. Satellites support current operations and gather data on adversaries. They also shape how forces share information and strike targets. The letter grows out of GAO's April 6, 2006 testimony on space acquisitions.

GAO set out the risks that drive cost growth and delay in space programs. Programs often begin before their technology is proven, which locks in trouble. GAO then listed keys to addressing those risks, drawn from top product developers. Chief among them is gathering knowledge before making big commitments. The letter gives Senate leaders a compact brief on a costly problem area.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-786r:
Oil and gas royalties from public lands are explained in GAO-06-786R, a letter report dated June 21, 2006. In fiscal year 2005, federal and Native American lands supplied about 35 percent of the oil and 26 percent of the natural gas produced in the United States. Firms that lease these lands pay royalties to the Minerals Management Service. The royalty is a set share of the value of what they produce. GAO explained why revenues lagged prices from 2001 to 2005.

GAO found that royalty revenues did not rise at the same pace as oil and gas prices. The main reason was that production volumes fell sharply in that span. Price, volume, and the royalty rate together decide total revenue. When volume drops, higher prices cannot fully fill the gap. The letter gives lawmakers a clear account of the math.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-876r:
United States policy work at the global lender is reviewed in GAO-06-876R, a letter report dated June 29, 2006. Congress has written dozens of mandates on United States policy toward the International Monetary Fund. They cover the positions the nation should push and how its director should vote on aid to borrowing nations. The Treasury Department must carry those mandates into the fund's debates. GAO checked whether Treasury's system for doing so still stands.

GAO found that Treasury has sustained its formal process for promoting United States policies. A task force links Treasury with the United States Executive Director at the fund. It spots early chances to shape member decisions. Since GAO's September 2005 report, the task force kept meeting on a regular basis. The letter confirms that a quiet piece of economic diplomacy stayed on track.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-926r:
Ski safety work and audited accounts meet in GAO letter GAO-06-926R, dated July 7, 2006, on the National Ski Patrol System. The patrol backs public safety in skiing, plus civic and learning aims. It is a federally chartered group, so law calls for audited yearly statements and a GAO read of them.

The audit reports cover the fiscal years that ended June 30, 2005 and 2004. The auditor judged the statements fairly shown, by U.S. accounting rules. GAO found no case of rule breaking that had to be reported. The letter tells Congress the audit duty for those years is met, with no flags raised.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1056r:
War costs owed by the Defense Department are tallied in GAO letter GAO-07-1056R, dated July 26, 2007. Since 2001 Congress has given hundreds of billions of dollars for the Global War on Terrorism. Reported yearly costs rose from about $0.2 billion in fiscal year 2001 to about $98.4 billion in fiscal year 2006.

For fiscal year 2007 Congress gave about $161.8 billion. The department sought $141.7 billion more for fiscal year 2008. GAO set out what drives future cost: pace of war, bases, troop moves, gear repair, and care for the hurt. The letter draws on the department's own monthly cost reports, and frames the trade-offs ahead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-246r:
More than a quarter of cars on U.S. roads run on at least one soft tire. GAO reported the costs of that neglect in GAO-07-246R, a letter dated February 9, 2007. The safety agency found a third of light trucks in the same state. Soft means 8 pounds per square inch or more below the maker's level. Tires lose 1 to 2 pounds a month on their own. Congress asked about safety, fuel waste, and fixes.

Soft tires played a role in 247 of 32,061 road deaths in 1999, the letter reports. Blowouts from soft tires kill about 41 people a year. The fuel penalty adds up across the fleet. Of 130 billion gallons burned in 2005, about 1.2 billion gallons were wasted. The letter reviews tire pressure monitoring systems now required on new vehicles. It also covers awareness campaigns and fleet maintenance rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-306r:
The space agency can lease out spare buildings and keep the rent under a test program. GAO reviewed the trial in GAO-07-306R, a letter dated March 1, 2007. Two centers, Ames and Kennedy, hold the leasing power. A 2005 law ordered this review before any expansion. GAO asked what money the power brought in. It asked whether deals needed the special power. It also checked controls and openness.

The trial produced about $1.3 million in benefits, GAO found. Lease income came to $972,546, with over $350,000 in work paid in kind. Most of it would not have reached the agency otherwise. One center spent about $480,000 of the rent on upkeep. Controls lagged the new freedom, GAO said. No test exists for whether leasing beats other options. No system tracks the value of in-kind rent. GAO urged a full policy before wider use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-326r: One audit in this chartered-corporation series carries a stated exception. GAO-07-326R, dated January 26, 2007, reviews the audit of the Pearl Harbor Survivors Association for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2005. The auditor found the statements fairly presented on a modified cash basis, with one exception. The auditor had not watched the year-end inventory count. The group's records did not allow later tests of inventory balances. GAO found no reportable noncompliance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-396r:
The Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) buys supplies for the armed forces through prime vendor contracts, and GAO report GAO-07-396R, dated February 26, 2007, checks the agency's fix-it plan for that program. Press reports in October 2005 raised doubts about the prices DLA paid. A House hearing followed, and DLA pledged a set of corrective actions.

GAO found the recent progress promising, but pricing flaws posed a lasting risk. Earlier reviews had cited weak oversight, poor pricing checks, and staff who lacked key skills. GAO urged the Secretary of Defense to have DLA confirm that every corrective action was done and working. The check was to be reported in writing within 6 months.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-416r:
A new security aid channel, Section 1206, is assessed in GAO-07-416R, issued February 28, 2007. The National Defense Authorization Act of 2006 let the Defense Department spend up to $200 million of its own funds to train and equip foreign forces. The aid targets counterterrorism and stability work. Supporters prize its speed. Critics say aid choices belong with the State Department.

GAO studied how the two departments pick recipient states and aid types. It traced how they shape and clear proposals together. It then checked how the programs run on the ground. The review drew on talks at embassies and combatant commands and on the law and agency guidance. The report gives Congress an early map of a fast-moving program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-476r:
American Gold Star Mothers honors sons and daughters lost in service, and its audit is reviewed in GAO-07-476R, dated March 9, 2007. The group's purposes include keeping alive the ideals of Americanism for which members' loved ones fought and died. As a federally chartered corporation, it must present yearly financial statements in detail. It must also obtain an audit by an outside public accountant.

GAO's letter covers the fiscal years ended June 30, 2005 and 2004. Staff read the audit reports and the statements and notes. Checks on the figures formed part of the work, though GAO did not audit the group itself. No reportable breach of the reporting law turned up. The auditors' opinions held that the statements were fairly presented under U.S. accounting standards. The review ends with the reports returned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-666r:
Historians keep a chartered association, and its books are reviewed in GAO-07-666R, a GAO letter released April 5, 2007. The American Historical Association promotes the study of history. It also gathers and preserves historical manuscripts. As a federally chartered corporation, it must file yearly statements of assets, debts, income, and costs. It must also obtain an audit by an outside public accountant under 36 U.S.C. 10101.

This letter reaches back three years, covering fiscal years ended June 30, 2004, 2003, and 2002. GAO read the audit reports and the statements and notes behind them. Checks on the numbers formed part of the work. GAO did not audit the association itself. The review found no reportable breach of the reporting law. The auditors' opinions held that the statements were fairly presented under U.S. accounting standards throughout.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-676r:
Does the U.S. public get a fair cut of its own oil and gas? GAO-07-676R, dated May 1, 2007, compares the take across owners. In fiscal year 2006, firms took over $77 billion from selling oil and gas from federal lands and waters. They paid the federal government about $10 billion in royalties. Alaska has just raised its state share. In January 2007, the Interior Department raised the royalty rate for future deepwater Gulf leases.

The letter writes up a March 2007 briefing for congressional staff. It sets the U.S. government take, the owner's share of a field's cash flow, beside that of other states and nations. It then models what higher royalty rates on future leases would yield. Terms vary widely by owner, the study shows, from bonuses to taxes. The point is a yardstick: Congress can weigh any rate hike against what peer owners charge.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-686r:
GAO-07-686R is a letter GAO sent on April 5, 2007, about the Department of Homeland Security's operations centers. Two laws told GAO to study the National Operations Center and centers run by DHS parts. GAO briefed House staff on March 1 and Senate staff on March 13, 2007. Both sets of staff said the briefing met the laws' demands. The letter passes that briefing on in written form. It rests on GAO's past report on the same centers.

The centers run 24 hours a day, every day of the year. They watch for threats and share facts during crises. GAO's past work found the centers gain from shared goals and clear roles. Joint plans and common rules also help them act as one. This letter says the centers would gain from more steps of that kind. It also notes GAO work under way on DHS plans to group its offices in the capital area.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-706r:
Guarding key national assets sector by sector is reviewed in GAO-07-706R, a letter dated July 10, 2007. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 wrecked oil sites, power lines, and phone towers on the Gulf Coast. The harm spread far past the storm zone. Private firms own about 85 percent of the nation's key assets. A national plan tells each sector to write its own guard plan. GAO read nine sector plans against the plan's rules.

The nine plans largely met those demands. Most set out goals, threat checks, and ways to rank assets by risk. Depth varied with how long each sector had worked as a group. Eight plans skipped one point, though. They did not say what lures would push owners to check their own risks. Such lures matter since many owners face no rules and act by choice. GAO urged the Homeland Security Department to state its data needs clearly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-796r:
Green cards for Haitian nationals are counted in GAO-07-796R, a report dated April 27, 2007. The Haitian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act of 1998 let many Haitians seek lawful permanent residence. Section 902(k) of the act orders a report every six months. GAO must count applications and approvals by category. Categories span asylum seekers, parolees, and orphaned or abandoned children. This is GAO's sixteenth report in the series.

Through March 31, 2007, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had received 40,844 applications. It had approved 17,538 of them. The Executive Office for Immigration Review had 2,020 applications filed. It had approved 797 of those. Most files move through a service center in Lincoln, Nebraska. Cases that need interviews go to local offices. The reports will run until every application is finally decided. Tables in the report break the counts down by each legal category.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-846r:
Services for victims of domestic violence and sexual assault fill GAO-07-846R, a report dated July 19, 2007. A 2005 law told GAO to study data on how common such crimes are. It named domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. Grants flow through 11 programs at two departments. They fund shelter, counseling, and legal help for victims. GAO checked what data grantees report on services. It asked how well the data show who gets help.

Grantees report service types and total victims served. Some report age and other traits of victims. Data do not show, for all services, how many men, women, youth, and children get each type. Laws for the 11 programs set unlike reporting rules. One agency lacks a standard form for its grantees. High staff turnover hurts data quality as well. GAO urged both departments to close the gaps. It also urged shared definitions for research. Both generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-886r:
A training center's business plan is critiqued in GAO-07-886R, a letter GAO sent on June 14, 2007. The National Transportation Safety Board opened the center in 2003. It trains accident investigators from the board and outside groups. In fiscal year 2006, costs topped revenues by $2.7 million. A 2006 law told the board to write a utilization plan. The draft arrived on March 28, 2007.

The draft plan would outsource the center's running to a vendor. The vendor would also build new courses and rent out spare space. Revenue would be shared with the board. The plan projects full cost coverage by the end of fiscal year 2010. GAO found thin support for its figures, though. It gives little rationale for a projected 10 percent revenue growth. Market analysis is left to the vendor to supply. The letter lists ways to firm up the plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-906r:
Two disability systems for wounded troops are compared in GAO-07-906R, a letter dated May 25, 2007. About 26,000 service members had been injured in Iraq and Afghanistan by April 2007. The Defense Department rates fitness and pays disability retirement. Veterans Affairs pays its own compensation after members leave service. In fiscal year 2005, the services judged over 23,000 cases. VA paid $34.5 billion to over 3.5 million people in fiscal year 2006. GAO briefed a presidential commission on April 23, 2007.

This letter presents the briefing's findings and open recommendations. Timeliness and consistency of military decisions draw concern. Training for medical and physical evaluation board staff needs review. VA claims processing shows backlogs and uneven ratings. Average wait and rating patterns vary across regions. GAO lists fixes it has already urged on both departments. The aim is one fair path from injury to benefits. The commission received the summary as it weighed reforms.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-306r:
Security fixes at an animal disease lab are tracked in GAO letter GAO-08-306R, dated December 17, 2007. Plum Island sits in Long Island Sound off New York. Its scientists study foreign animal diseases, some deadly to livestock and a few to people. Foot-and-mouth disease is the chief fear. The island lab passed from the agriculture department to the security department after the terrorist attacks on the United States.

Past reviews left a list of security recommendations for the site. GAO checked how many have been carried out. The title reports real headway: the department has put most fixes in place. Several recommendations remain open, though. The letter keeps them in plain view.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-316r:
In GAO letter report GAO-08-316R, dated January 22, 2008, GAO reviews an Army equipment maintenance contract in Kuwait. Under Task Order 1, a contractor at Camp Arifjan repaired vehicles such as Bradley Fighting Vehicles and Humvees for forces in Iraq and Afghanistan. GAO assessed the contractor's work and the Army's oversight of it.

For five vehicle types inspected from July 2006 through May 2007, 18 to 31 percent of equipment offered as ready failed government inspection. Rework after failed inspections added about 188,000 hours and about $4.2 million in cost. GAO also found errors in the contractor's maintenance database and gaps in Army quality assurance. GAO concluded that the Army needs to put an effective management and oversight plan in place for the contract.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-576r:
Retirement systems modernization at the personnel agency is covered in GAO comment letter GAO-08-576R, dated March 28, 2008. The Office of Personnel Management is replacing paper-heavy retirement processing for federal workers. In January 2008, GAO flagged four weak areas: system testing, defect fixing, cost estimation, and earned value tracking.

Congress ordered the agency to report its fixes by February 20, 2008, and ordered GAO to comment. GAO found the reply thin in places. On testing, the agency spoke mainly to one test phase and reported 74 percent of scenarios passed, short of its own goal. Defect data showed a growing backlog of problems to clear before launch. The letter walks through each of the four areas and presses for fuller answers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-606r:
Since the 1940s, the Department of Energy and the agencies before it have enriched uranium for weapons and reactors. That work left behind large piles of depleted uranium, called tails. In GAO-08-606R, a report dated March 31, 2008, GAO looked at what the department could do with the tails and what they might be worth.

GAO listed three broad options: sell the tails as they are, enrich them again, or store them for good. About one-third of the tails hold enough uranium-235 to enrich again at a profit. GAO found the department likely lacks legal power to sell the raw tails under a 1996 law. The department had not yet finished a full review of the choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-736r:
Commanders in Iraq got a fast cash fund to fix urgent local needs, from water to schools. The Commander's Emergency Response Program sits inside more than $46 billion for Iraq relief since fiscal year 2003. GAO-08-736R, a letter dated June 23, 2008, reviews how projects get picked and watched.

Broad rules give commanders wide freedom to choose projects, which fits the fund's quick-help aim. But loose guidance can scatter money across unlike projects with weak follow-up. Teamwork with aid and engineering agencies also needs work. GAO calls for clearer pick rules and tighter oversight, while keeping the speed that makes the fund useful on the ground.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-836r:
Federal Reserve Banks run key money systems for the Treasury's debt office. GAO-08-836R, a letter dated June 16, 2008, reports flaws in the computer security controls at those banks. The work came out of the yearly audit of the federal debt schedules for fiscal years 2007 and 2006.

Core controls still held up overall, and the flaws found were not classed as major gaps. Guards, activity watch tools, and hand cross-checks blunted the risk. Still, GAO lists the weak spots that bank leaders should fix. It also checks on fixes promised after past audits of the same systems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-846r:
Selling airwaves for new wireless services forced federal users to move frequencies. A 2004 law set up a fund to pay those moving costs. One agency, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, first drew about $3.6 million, then got more than $35 million more. GAO-08-846R, a letter dated September 9, 2008, judges the reason given for that jump.

The first request missed many real costs, GAO found: extra gear, offices, systems, and a fifth frequency assignment. The homeland security department and the agency both failed to spot the gaps. Extra duties punish imports sold too cheaply or propped up by foreign aid. Since fiscal year 2001, hundreds of millions in such duties went uncollected. GAO-08-876R, a letter dated July 24, 2008, reports agency views on fixing collection through world trade deals.

By March 2008 the uncollected sum topped $600 million. Four causes drive the loss, the letter notes. Agencies told GAO that stronger world agreements would be hard to win and weak in effect. Importers owe the duties, and many sit abroad beyond easy reach. The letter gives Congress the agencies' blunt verdict before it weighs new treaty pushes.
